title: Capstone: Command-Line Task Manager
learningObjectives: Model tasks with unique identifiers and completion state
Combine classes and collections to implement task operations
Implement add, list and complete commands with input validation
Persist task data and restore it safely when the program restarts
Test duplicate identifiers, malformed storage and unknown commands

understand.concept: Separate task data, application logic, persistence and console interaction. Build one feature at a time and test empty storage, duplicate IDs, invalid commands and file errors.
understand.whyItMatters: A capstone combines domain modelling, collections, command parsing, file persistence, validation and modular design. Splitting responsibilities makes the program easier to test and change than putting every feature into one large main method.
understand.analogy: A task manager resembles a small office: the console receives requests, the service applies rules, the repository stores records, and each Task represents one item of work.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not define software boundaries. Choose classes and interfaces based on responsibilities, dependencies and testability rather than creating a class for every noun.

explain.narrative:
## Capstone goal and separation of responsibilities

Build a command-line task manager that supports adding, listing, completing and removing tasks, plus help and exit commands. Separate task data, business rules, persistence and console interaction. This separation makes the project easier to test and prevents file handling from becoming mixed with menu logic.

## Suggested design

- `Task`: task ID, nonblank title and completion state.
- `TaskService`: validates commands and enforces unique IDs and valid state transitions.
- `TaskRepository`: loads and saves records using a documented UTF-8 format.
- `Main`: reads console input, dispatches commands and displays results.

Choose whether task IDs are generated or supplied. Define how duplicate IDs, blank titles, unknown commands, missing tasks and malformed saved records are handled. Avoid parsing a delimiter-based format without an escaping rule; titles may contain the delimiter or newline.

## Persistence and failure safety

Load existing tasks at startup and save successful changes. For safer replacement, write a complete new snapshot to a temporary file and move it over the previous file only after writing succeeds. Handle unsupported atomic moves where necessary. Do not print “saved” until the write has completed.

## Acceptance tests

Start with empty storage, add two tasks, complete one, list them, remove one, exit and restart. Confirm the remaining state is correct. Also test duplicate IDs, blank titles, malformed records, unknown commands, a missing task ID and a file access failure. The project is complete when the behavior is predictable after restart, not merely when a single in-memory list prints.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { record Task(int id, String title, boolean done) {} Task t = new Task(1, "Write tests", false); System.out.println(t.title()); } }
examples.explanation: Models a task as an immutable record.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.List<String> tasks = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); tasks.add("Plan"); tasks.add("Build"); System.out.println(tasks); } }
examples.explanation: Stores tasks in an ordered list.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Map<Integer,String> tasks = new java.util.LinkedHashMap<>(); tasks.put(1, "Review"); System.out.println(tasks.containsKey(1)); } }
examples.explanation: Uses a stable ID to look up a task.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String command = "complete"; System.out.println(switch(command) { case "add", "list", "complete" -> "known command"; default -> "unknown command"; }); } }
examples.explanation: Validates a command before dispatching an action.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.nio.file.Path p = java.nio.file.Files.createTempFile("tasks", ".txt"); try { java.nio.file.Files.writeString(p, "1|Plan|false"); System.out.println(java.nio.file.Files.readString(p)); } finally { java.nio.file.Files.deleteIfExists(p); } } }
examples.explanation: Demonstrates a simple persistence record; a production project should validate fields and handle escaping.

practise.guidedTask: Model a Task with an ID, title and completion state. Implement add, list and complete commands using a Map and reject duplicate IDs.
practise.independentTask: Build the command-line task manager with separate Task, TaskService, TaskRepository and Main classes. Persist tasks in a documented UTF-8 text format.
hints: Keep task rules in TaskService and file operations in TaskRepository; keep Main focused on input and display.
Define an escaping or structured serialization format so titles containing delimiters cannot corrupt saved records.
Test the full add/complete/remove/restart journey and verify that failed saves do not report success.
practise.challenge: Test empty storage, malformed records, duplicate IDs, unknown commands, completing a missing task and restarting after saved changes.

questions.prompt: Which separation makes a task manager easier to maintain?
options: Task model, application logic, persistence and console interface
All code inside main with global variables
File operations inside every print statement
Mixing input parsing with ID generation
questions.answer: Task model, application logic, persistence and console interface
questions.explanation: Separating task data, business rules, persistence and console interaction keeps each part focused and independently testable.

questions.prompt: What should happen when a task ID does not exist?
options: Report that the task was not found without changing other tasks
questions.answer: Report that the task was not found without changing other tasks
questions.explanation: An unknown task ID should produce a not-found result and must not mutate unrelated tasks.

options: Tasks remain available after the application exits
It removes the need for validation
questions.answer: Tasks remain available after the application exits
questions.explanation: Persistence stores task state outside process memory so the data can be loaded again after the application restarts.

questions.prompt: Which collection is suitable for looking up tasks by unique ID?
questions.explanation: A Map is appropriate when each task is retrieved by a unique ID key.

questions.prompt: Which scenario belongs in capstone testing?
options: Loading an empty file and handling malformed or missing data
Deleting source code after each run
questions.answer: Loading an empty file and handling malformed or missing data
questions.explanation: A robust capstone test includes empty storage, malformed records and missing task data, not only a successful in-memory command.
